newsitem.title: UK: UK M4 brings inflation warning, despite distortions.
newsitem.headline: UK M4 brings inflation warning, despite distortions.

text.p: Despite its tarnished reputation as a key inflation indicator, a spurt in British broad money supply in February adds to mounting evidence of a pick up in economic activity and growing price pressures.
The Bank of England said on Thursday that M4 -- the broad measure of British money supply -- grew by 11.3 percent in the year to February, after an upwardly revised rate of 10 percent in January.
This pushed the indicator even further beyond the government's monitoring range of three to nine percent, which has already been exceeded for more than a year.

Economists say that while broad money has been distorted by special factors in the last two years, its enduring strength shows confidence among corporates and households is growing and points to increased borrowing and spending in the months ahead.
"The M4 and bank lending figures are very noisy, but they fit in with the picture painted by other data showing activity is picking up pace," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.

"Unemployment is falling, retail spending is growing at a decent rate, borrowing for house purchases is robust and corporate borrowing is strong. The economy is well passed the point in the business cycle where it can enjoy both strong growth and low inflation."
M4 comprises all bank and building society deposits, corporate and personal, as well as cash in the hands of the public. It includes the entire stock of household mortgage debt.
The broad money aggregate had its heyday in the late 1980s when rapid growth correctly signalled the subsequent housing and consumer boom.
But in the last two years, the predictive powers of M4 have been eroded. It has been swollen by a surge in corporate takeover activity and, more recently, the introduction of the gilt repo market.

"M4 has not been a good leading indicator of domestic demand over the past few years and has been distorted by the introduction of the gilt repo market," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS. "But such a high figure is cause for concern."
He said it adds weight to evidence of a stronger labour market and retail sales released on Wednesday which, taken together, suggest monetary policy is too slack.
M4 figures, along with the rest of this week's data, will reinforce the case made by Bank of England governor Eddie George, who has been arguing for higher interest rates since late last year.

He has repeatedly expressed concern about the fast growth of broad money supply and believes interest rates should be raised by a quarter point to 6.25 percent immediately if the government is to hit its inflation target of 2.5 percent.
But with a general election due on May 1, the chances of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke agreeing to a rate rise at the next monetary meeting on April 10 look slim.
"Clarke would have to be a saint to raise rates now," said Mackie.

Inflation data, also out on Thursday, played into the Chancellor's hands. They showed retail prices headed lower in February with targeted underlying inflation edging down to 2.9 percent from 3.1 percent in January.
Some economists say that stripped of its distortions, M4 paints a much more subdued picture of domestic demand.
Simon Briscoe, economist at Nikko, said while the figures suggest a stronger economy than initially thought, one month does not make a trend.
"Sharp rises in the past have been followed by equally sharp falls, most notably at the start of last year. We await further evidence before being convinced."
